text: Never commit straight to develop/main. Cut a fresh branch from main, land via PR, and don't open the PR unless asked.
No silent failures. If a required input is missing or an assumption breaks, raise a clear error instead of degrading silently or guessing a default.

Match the repo's existing conventions — comment density, docstring format, naming, import idioms. Analyze a repo's style at most ONCE (the first time you work in it) and save a short note to .alexs-rig/style.md; on later work, read that note and follow it instead of re-analyzing. Never impose a different style. Roboflow repos: follow Piotr Skalski (SkalskiP) standards via the skalskip-review skill.
When a result changes a conclusion, update the report or table with the precise numbers. Don't leave the document stale while narrating the correction in chat.
If a request rests on a wrong premise, say so instead of implementing around it. Correcting the premise is more useful than accommodating it.

When comparing methods, spend equal effort on every arm — if one side gets tuned parameters, a matched knob, or a favourable default, the others get the same. This includes the measuring apparatus itself: warm-up, ordering and allocation must not favour an arm. If the result changes when you swap the order of the arms, the measurement is biased, not the code. State any remaining asymmetry explicitly; a reviewer will find it otherwise.

Work through the agreed plan without stopping for trivial confirmations, but ask for explicit confirmation before heavy or outward-facing git actions (opening PRs, pushing, merging) and before any change that alters results or behavior. Read-only and additive work proceeds without asking.

Verify against the real source (implementation, paper, docs) before asserting a fact or claiming done — don't guess or invent. Report honestly: no false precision, no claiming verified or done without evidence.

Do exactly what's asked with the simplest, most generalizable solution — no scope, abstractions or options that weren't requested, and prefer shorter when behavior is unchanged. Keep changes additive and surgical: don't move, rename or restructure existing code or params to accomplish a task; add alongside and flag if a rename seems needed.

When you replace something, remove what it replaced: the old code path, superseded tests, imports that no longer resolve to anything. Check what depended on the change. Every artifact left behind must earn its place — a second test covering behavior an existing test already covers does not.

Before hand-rolling a primitive, check whether the framework or an existing module already provides it; if swapping, prove equivalence with numbers (values and gradients) and preserve any guard the builtin lacks. Check our own modules too: two classes doing the same job, or a piece sitting in the wrong layer, is the same duplication.

Before calling anything done, exercise it: run every code path end to end at least once through the entry point the product actually uses — a test that re-implements the path it claims to cover is not coverage — then inspect what it produced (open the video, confirm where the files landed, check which tool or model actually ran). If you changed something that already worked, re-check the specific cases that motivated the earlier fixes: a new fix must not silently undo an old one. Report what was actually run and what you checked.

Paid compute is the last step, not a debugging surface. BEFORE: validate every new metric, formula and code path on a free tiny local case — a fraction >1, a bad broadcast, a saturated statistic are all catchable there; then state instance, VRAM and cost, and pick the cheapest config that answers the question. DURING: a launch that hangs or returns ambiguously is NOT a started run — confirm the process is alive and making real progress in the log, and never poll without a hard timeout. AFTER: pull the run's config, parameters and results off the machine BEFORE stopping it — any number you may cite later has to survive the VM, and a result you cannot reproduce is not a result. Then stop it and verify nothing is left assigned.

Land changes where they belong and ship a clean diff. Confirm you are on the intended branch before editing, and before pushing read the diff: it must contain only what belongs to this PR — no stray local files, no unrelated edits, no work that belongs to a different PR in the stack. A problem found while the introducing PR is still open gets fixed in that PR, not patched downstream.

A correction paid for once is paid for everywhere: when the user corrects style, content, or method, apply it to all sibling artifacts and all future work unprompted, and fold recurring review criteria into the relevant skill.

A performance or optimization claim must show the whole trade-off: time AND memory, measured, against the previous method, on comparable hardware — an optimization shown on one axis only is not a result.

Answer the question that was asked, in the same turn and in plain language. If you need to verify first, give the direct answer first and the verification after. Unpack jargon rather than assuming it lands — a term the reader has to ask about is a term you should have explained.
